summary: SOL 5111 is an interactive, browser-based Mars outpost simulator designed to teach students real space engineering trade-offs through crisis survival. Grounded in authentic NASA telemetry from Opportunity, Curiosity, Phoenix, and MRO, the simulation challenges players to balance power generation, life support, radiation shielding, and food production on a single constrained Martian power grid over seven sols.
details:
Overview & Challenge Alignment

Most educational space games either oversimplify physics—allowing students to run every system simultaneously with unlimited energy—or present raw aerospace telemetry that overwhelms middle and high school learners. SOL 5111 bridges this gap by placing students in the role of a junior engineer responsible for maintaining a Martian outpost during a planet-encircling dust storm until a rescue shuttle arrives at the end of Sol 7.

How It Works

Players manage six interconnected facilities—Solar Array, Storage, Habitat, Greenhouse, Regolith Site, and Shelter—sharing a single finite power grid:

• Guided Discovery Tutorial: Before the seven-sol mission timer starts, learners explore the outpost in a zero-pressure sandbox. They test greenhouse lighting modes (Dim at 0.33 u/s vs. Bright at 1.30 u/s) and observe real-time quantitative trade-offs between crop harvest time and battery survival at peak dust.

• Dynamic Resource Triage: As dust opacity rises, solar input drops drastically. Students must connect spare batteries, monitor consumption rates (u/s), and make hard choices—such as temporarily shutting down the water recycler to keep the landing beacon powered at touchdown.

• Regolith Diagnostic Loop: When dust breaches the greenhouse dome, toxic perchlorates spike and halt crop growth. Players must seal the hull, collect soil samples at the regolith site, and analyze them in the Habitat lab to unlock decontamination.

• Radiation Shielding Trade-Off: During solar particle events, players must move the astronaut into the shielded Shelter to limit radiation exposure, sacrificing the ability to perform outdoor repairs while balancing shelter ventilation power.

• Post-Mission Engineering Debrief: Instead of an arbitrary score, the simulator audits every critical decision made during the run (timestamps, power saved, exposure dose, and sensor telemetry) and awards an engineering rank up to Mission Commander.

Technical Architecture & Accessibility

• Zero-Dependency Web Stack: Built with pure HTML5, CSS3, and modular Vanilla ES6+ JavaScript (engine.js, world.js, game.js, languages.js, avatar.js). The deterministic physics and resource core (engine.js) is completely decoupled from the DOM.

• Classroom Ready: Hosted on GitHub Pages with instant loading (<1s) and zero installation required, ensuring compatibility with school Chromebooks and low-end devices.

• Inclusive & Bilingual: Supports full keyboard navigation (WASD/Arrows), ARIA accessibility attributes, astronaut customization, and instant switching between English and Ukrainian.

• Progressive Curriculum: Features two missions—Dust on the Horizon (core survival and diagnostics) and The Long Storm (extended energy deficits and dual-tray crop planning).
